title: Spider-Man's New Villain Was Almost the Shadow King Instead of Jean Grey
summary: When you're making the fourth Spider-Man movie with Tom Holland, you have a problem: most of the famous villains are already used. So the writers of 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' had to dig deeper. Co-writer Chris McKenna revealed on the 'Bulwark Goes Hollywood' podcast that they almost used the Shadow King, an X-Men villain who possesses people and controls their powers. The Shadow King, also known as Amahl Farouk, is a psychic parasite created by Chris Claremont and John Byrne. In the comics, he was the first evil mutant Professor Xavier ever met. McKenna even had a cool plan: Spider-Man would only communicate with the Shadow King by possessing people, like in 'Die Hard with a Vengeance' where John McClane talks to the villain only by phone. But Marvel Studios, which owns the X-Men characters, said no. They didn't even want the villain called 'Shadow King' or 'Farouk.' So the writers switched to Jean Grey, played by Sadie Sink. In the final movie, Jean's telepathy works a lot like the Shadow King's would have — she leaps between people, making them puppets of her will. It feels more like possession than simple mind control. McKenna explained that the villain choices were limited because Kraven the Hunter and the Chameleon were off-limits due to Sony's Spider-Man Universe. Once they decided on a telepathic villain, they entered mutant territory. Marvel approved Jean Grey around September 2024. So the movie we got almost had a completely different bad guy — and knowing that makes some scenes feel different. If the Shadow King had made it in, Spider-Man would have faced a villain who never shows his real face, speaking only through innocent people. Instead, Jean Grey brings that same creepy puppet-master energy to the screen. Either way, the writers had to solve a puzzle: how do you scare an audience with a villain they've never heard of? Their answer was to borrow a page from the X-Men's world — and it almost went to a completely different character.
why_it_matters: For teenagers who follow superhero films, this shows that what reaches the screen is decided as much by contracts and character ownership as by storytelling — the same corporate rules that shape music samples, game crossovers and streaming libraries.

background_read: The rights to Spider-Man are split: Sony Pictures has owned the film rights since the 1990s and makes the solo movies, while Marvel Studios — the Disney-owned company behind the Avengers films — helps produce them. Because two studios share the character, each one controls which villains and side characters are allowed to appear.

The X-Men are a team of mutant superheroes created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby in the 1960s. Their film rights belonged to 20th Century Fox for years, but Disney bought Fox, which is how Marvel Studios ended up in charge of those characters — and why a writer had to ask permission to use one.

Jean Grey is one of the original X-Men and is most famous for the Phoenix storyline, in which her huge psychic powers turn dangerous. The Shadow King, also called Amahl Farouk, was created by writer Chris Claremont and artist John Byrne during their celebrated X-Men run in the late 1970s; in those stories he was the first evil mutant Charles Xavier ever met.
Sadie Sink is an American actress best known for playing Max in the Netflix series Stranger Things.

perspectives.description: Now that Marvel Studios controls the X-Men, writers can finally borrow from that world, and Jean Grey's possession-style telepathy gives the film a genuinely creepy villain. Fans of both franchises get a crossover they waited years for.

McKenna's story suggests studio vetoes squeezed the writers: they were blocked from the character and even from the names. The result may look like a compromise rather than a first-choice creative decision.

Long-running franchises have always been governed by who holds which rights — Sony controls Spider-Man's solo films while Marvel controls the X-Men. When the biggest villains are used up, sequels either reinvent old foes or import characters from other corners of the same universe.

As Disney folds the X-Men deeper into its shared film universe, more mutant heroes and villains will cross over, so the Shadow King idea may return in another project. Future Spider-Man films will probably rely even more openly on characters owned by their partner studio.
